| Enumeration | Small, finite legal spaces where every candidate can be checked. | Explicit action space and affordable complete coverage. | Used after the space has grown beyond the available budget. |
| Random search or sampling | Large spaces that permit independent samples and need a transparent control. | Legal sampler, matched budget, and retained failures. | Treated as protection against a poor objective or representation. |
| Deterministic heuristics | Spaces with useful domain structure that can reduce search transparently. | Stated rule, assumptions, and stopping condition. | Hidden tuning or a rule whose bias excludes the useful region. |
| Bayesian optimization | Expensive black-box evaluations in low or moderate dimension where a useful surrogate and acquisition rule can be maintained. | Compatible observations, a checked surrogate and acquisition rule, and a sequential budget. | Highly combinatorial or shifting space with a poor surrogate. |
| Differentiable optimization | Continuous parameters or a trustworthy differentiable relaxation of a discrete problem. | Useful gradients and a plan to check the relaxed solution after discretization or implementation. | Proxy or relaxation gap makes the gradient point toward an unrealizable or inferior design. |
| Evolutionary search | Discrete or mixed spaces, populations, mutation/crossover structure, parallel evaluations. | Legal variation operators and enough evaluation budget. | Evaluation hunger, opaque tuning, weak comparison to random/local search. |
| Reinforcement learning | Sequential state-action problems with repeated related tasks and delayed feedback. | A state representation that preserves the information needed to predict the next state and reward after an action, plus a meaningful reward, many interactions or transfer, and a stable simulator. | Treating a static one-shot parameter search as RL without a sequential advantage. |
| Mathematical programming, constraint solving, or program synthesis/search | Algebraic objectives, discrete choices, or precisely specified legality and construction rules. | Executable objectives, constraints, or program semantics. | Broad architectural desirability that cannot be represented by the formulation. |

: **Search-procedure selection matches the design-space structure and feedback
cost.** No procedure is universally superior; the choice depends on the
cost of evaluation and the structure of the parameter space.
{#tbl-optimization-methods tbl-colwidths="[20,28,26,26]"}

Search procedures differ in structural fit, required conditions, and the
mismatches that should rule them out. Enumeration, sampling, and
deterministic heuristics fit spaces that can be covered or reduced directly.
Bayesian methods need observations from matching conditions and a useful
surrogate.
Evolutionary methods do not require that fitted surrogate, but they do need
legal variation operators and enough new evaluations to support population
search. Reinforcement learning needs a genuinely sequential state-action
problem, while solver-backed search needs executable objectives or properties.
The mismatch column is decisive because a familiar method name does not repair
a space, objective, or feedback path that violates its assumptions.

Every learned optimizer needs a strong simple comparison under the same legal
space, tool path, and evaluation budget. Enumeration is the comparison for a
small finite set. Random search is often useful in larger spaces because it
requires no learned surrogate and parallelizes easily
[@BergstraBengio2012RandomSearch]. A deterministic heuristic may be stronger
when domain structure is available. Random search can still optimize a poor
proxy or a badly represented space, so it is a transparent control rather than
a guarantee of correctness.

PrefixRL illustrates a tighter sequential formulation. It casts
parallel-prefix circuits as a reinforcement-learning problem with logic
synthesis in the evaluation path [@RoyEtAl2021PrefixRL]. The declared circuit
space and synthesis feedback make the method inspectable, but the result still
depends on the objective, tool conditions, and matched baseline.

An optimizer should stop when its budget is spent, the decision is stable,
required inputs become unavailable, the feasible region is empty under the
declared constraints, or another evaluation is unlikely to change the
decision enough to justify its cost. The execution request should ask the
environment to retain why each evaluation was selected and how the method
compared with the simpler alternative.

## Combining Methods Without a Fixed Order {#sec-one-model-specialists-hybrid}

There is no universal prediction-to-generation-to-optimization order. Start
where the problem's missing capability lies and move as tool feedback changes
the work. Deterministic schemas and scripts can enforce legal formats,
analytical models can estimate consequences, compilers can construct
transformations, and direct tools can evaluate candidates. Add another
component only when it performs necessary work that the existing path cannot
perform economically.

A predictor may condition a generator before construction, screen artifacts
after generation, or sit inside an optimizer as a surrogate. An optimizer may
control a generator, select among existing candidates, or use direct tool
feedback with no predictor. A generator may revise an artifact after a compiler
or simulator return. Any family may be absent, and feedback can send the work
back to whichever component owns the required change.

Generation, prediction, and optimization are not automatically a three-stage
pipeline. They combine only when the problem contains distinct jobs
(@tbl-method-organization). AutoTVM combines schedule templates, learned cost
prediction, simulated-annealing search, and target measurement
[@ChenEtAl2018AutoTVM]. Ansor combines program construction, learned cost
prediction, evolutionary search, compilation, and target measurement
[@ZhengEtAl2020Ansor]. In these systems, schedule or program construction
proposes candidates, the learned cost model predicts their likely performance,
simulated-annealing or evolutionary search selects candidates, and compilation
plus target measurement checks them. The mapping shows distinct roles, method
families, and implementations inside tensor-program tuning; it does not
establish a required three-stage architecture workflow. KernelBench needs
generation and a harness but not a learned optimizer. A small enumerated study
may need none of the three.

Other engineering roles can surround these compositions. A critique may
identify a missing AXI ordering assumption. A learned method, script, or
engineer may return a repaired artifact. Interface and implementation tools
check stated properties. A harness coordinates compatible RTL, compiler,
workload, and tool state. An analysis method or architect explains whether data
movement, computation, or another mechanism changed the system result. These
roles produce the different outputs in @tbl-method-role-handoffs, but critique,
repair, checking, explanation, and coordination are not additional method
families. None of them must be performed by a learned component.

Component boundaries should follow method fit rather than the number of roles.
One component may perform several roles when its inputs, outputs, allowed
actions, cost, stopping conditions, and required checks remain clear. Split
the work when those requirements differ or when a shared component would judge
assumptions it created itself. A split adds a handoff and does not by itself
make the judgment independent. Any claim of independence must be supported by
a sufficiently different execution, checking, or review path together with
the shared assumptions that remain. The study should name which requirements,
data, code, tools, and failure modes are shared and which differ. The resulting
combinations differ in when they are justified and in what keeps them minimal
(@tbl-method-organization).

| **Composition** | **When it is justified** | **What keeps it minimal** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Conventional technique or direct tools | Existing calculations, builders, solvers, heuristics, or evaluations can perform the job economically. | Add no learned component unless it removes distinct work without weakening the check. |
| Generation only | Useful artifacts are missing and direct checking is affordable. | Stop when enough useful candidates exist or review becomes limiting. |
| Prediction only | Existing candidates need cheap screening before costly evaluation. | Retain the predictor only while qualification and confirmation cost less than direct evaluation. |
| Optimization only | A declared objective can guide selection over a space too large to enumerate. | Compare with a strong simple baseline and stop when further selection cannot change the decision economically. |
| Generation plus prediction | Candidate construction is needed, but most proposals cannot afford direct evaluation. | The predictor screens only the consequence for which compatible support exists. |
| Generation plus optimization | Candidate construction is needed, and the evaluation budget requires selective search, but no supported surrogate is available. | The optimizer uses direct feedback and each generated candidate still passes the declared checks. |
| Prediction plus optimization | A surrogate makes selective search economical under expensive feedback. | Keep the surrogate, acquisition rule, and later confirmation separately inspectable. |
| Generation, prediction, and optimization | Missing artifacts, costly evaluation, and selective search all limit the same study. | Each component has a distinct input, output, action, cost, and stopping condition. |

: **A component earns its place by performing necessary work that another
component does not.** Adding more models or agents is not itself a stronger
method. {#tbl-method-organization tbl-colwidths="[24,38,38]"}

@tbl-method-organization is a supporting comparison for the canonical recipe,
not a second selection sequence. It does not prescribe an order or reward a
larger composition. A composition applies only when each named job is missing
and its stopping condition keeps every added component economical.

## Worked Method Decisions

The worked cases support the canonical recipe by testing opposite outcomes, a
multi-component compiler-tuning composition and direct tool use for the
Lighthouse cache study. Candidate construction, cost prediction, selective
search, and target measurement can be plausible when the legal schedule space
is too large for direct measurement, but a new study still needs a fixed
operator, target, conventional comparator, and matched budget before selecting
that composition.

The Lighthouse cache study has the opposite shape. Its three cache-capacity
settings already define the candidate set, and its budget covers a direct SRAM
screen followed by matched cycle-level evaluation. A generator would construct
nothing missing, a predictor would need observations that the study does not
have, and an optimizer would add search to a three-point comparison. The
comparison in @tbl-worked-method-decisions retains the exact decision fields
behind these different choices.

### Compiler Tuning and Direct Cache Evaluation

| **Decision field** | **Compiler-tuning candidate** | **Lighthouse cache study** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Job** | Construct or select a schedule that improves a declared operator on a named target. | Compare the specified 2\ MiB baseline setting with the proposed 3\ MiB and 4\ MiB settings without widening the study. |
| **Inputs and support** | Would require a fixed operator or workload, target hardware, legal schedule or program space, compiler state, observations from matching conditions, and an evaluation budget. | Three proposed `l2.capacity` settings, declared hardware, software, and workload identities, specified SRAM limits, and no retained observations from matching conditions. |
| **Approach status** | A plausible composition may use AutoTVM-style schedule templates, a learned cost model, and simulated-annealing search, or Ansor-style program construction, learned cost prediction, and evolutionary search. The choice remains open until its comparator and budget are fixed. | Use direct evaluation as the next action once the proposed configurations and tool path are executable. Request the declared SRAM screen followed by matched cycle-level evaluations for eligible settings. Add no generator, predictor, or optimizer. |
| **Output and legal actions** | Return an accepted schedule and its measured target result. Change only fields in the declared schedule or program space. | A future run would return modeled SRAM properties and matched cycle-level results. It may select only `l2.capacity` values `2MiB`, `3MiB`, or `4MiB` and may change no other architecture or software field. |
| **Evaluator and later checks** | The compiler and target measurements evaluate selected schedules under common semantics and conditions. | The planned `SRAM-A` step would screen declared physical limits. Planned `SIM-A`, `CACHE-A`, and `PM-A` steps would return the matched system results needed for the later comparison. |
| **Feedback cost** | Must count cost-model fitting, candidate construction, search, compilation, target runs, and tuning review under a matched budget that has not yet been declared. | The declared budget allows three SRAM evaluations, at most four cycle-level executions including infrastructure reruns, configuration checks, and review. No execution cost has been incurred. |
| **Fallback and stop** | A credible conventional comparator, matched budget, fallback, and stopping rule must be fixed before deciding whether the composition is justified. None is selected here. | If the configurations and tool path become executable, compare all capacities directly without the SRAM screen if necessary. Stop when the decision is resolved, the eligible set is exhausted, the cycle-level budget is spent, a required input is unavailable, or no alternative passes the SRAM limits. |

: **The missing capability determines the composition.** Compiler tuning can
plausibly need construction, prediction, and selective search when target
measurements are costly, but the choice remains conditional on a comparator and
budget fixed before results are known. The cache study already specifies its
parameter settings and a direct-evaluation budget.
{#tbl-worked-method-decisions tbl-colwidths="[18,41,41]"}

These fields resolve the approach choice for the Lighthouse cache study, not
its architecture result. Compiler tuning remains conditional because the
strongest practical conventional alternative must be selected for the actual
operator and target rather than inferred from a generic method label. A
compiler default, optimized library, expert schedule, or conventional
autotuner should be fixed before learned tuning begins. The same rule applies
to the prospective KernelBench comparison, where the strongest practical
conventional constructor remains unresolved.

### Lighthouse Cache Study Handoff

@tbl-lighthouse-approach-decision is the complete method-side handoff. It
retains the selected approach, allowed change, required tool roles, cost
envelope, and necessary checks. @sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces
owns the environment mechanics that carry this boundary into real tools.

| **Handoff field** | **`XR-L2-CAP-A` method decision** |
| --- | --- |
| **Selected approach** | Use direct evaluation with *no added method*. Add no generator, predictor, or optimizer because the three proposed capacities already define the complete candidate set. |
| **Allowed change** | Change only `l2.capacity` among `2MiB`, `3MiB`, and `4MiB`; keep the declared hardware, software, workload, cache policy, memory system, and exclusions fixed. Any other architecture or software change reopens the study. |
| **Required tool roles** | `SRAM-A` under `PVT-A` screens macro area and access time and supplies cache energy and leakage estimates. `SIM-A` with `CACHE-A` and `PM-A` measures matched frame-time, miss, and subsystem-power consequences. |
| **Cost envelope** | Allow three SRAM evaluations and at most four cycle-level executions including infrastructure reruns, plus the declared configuration checks and review. |
| **Necessary checks and fallback** | Confirm candidate and condition identity. Reject capacities above 3\ W modeled subsystem power, 1.5\ mm^2^ macro area, or 2.5\ ns modeled access time. At most one candidate may advance, and only if its physical checks pass and its qualified interval relative to the 2\ MiB rerun baseline lies above zero. Thermal and IR-drop reviews remain independent later requirements. If the SRAM screen is unavailable, the fallback is a matched direct comparison of all three capacities within the same cycle-level budget. @sec-feedback-verification-trust owns interval qualification. |

: **Direct evaluation is the defensible starting choice for the Lighthouse
cache study.** The declared problem has three proposed settings, no live
history from matching conditions, and a declared budget for the SRAM screen
and cycle-level comparison. No total-cost comparison has established that an
added method would be cheaper.
{#tbl-lighthouse-approach-decision tbl-colwidths="[21,69]"}

The SRAM screen may protect scarce cycle-level evaluations, but it cannot
interpret the later system result. The no-added-method choice should be
revisited only if the legal cache space expands, direct evaluation becomes the
limiting cost, and observations from matching conditions become available.
The study rejects an unnecessary method, not AI-assisted architecture as a
whole.

## Open Research Questions

**Prospective approach selection.** A fair study needs measurable ways to
choose the approach and comparator before results are known.

- **How accurately can a prospective method-cost model identify when a learned
  component will reduce total design effort?** The research object is a
  study-level estimate of setup, data preparation, qualification, execution,
  checking, and review cost from information available before work begins. Its
  evaluation can report held-out cost error and calibration, and the extra
  realized cost caused by choices made with the estimate.

- **Can a pre-execution comparator-selection procedure choose a credible
  conventional approach without access to the learned result?** The procedure
  must account for the task, target, tools, budget, and available expertise.
  Evaluation can measure agreement with blinded expert selections, the chosen
  comparator's realized result and total cost, and how often later blinded
  reselection changes the study conclusion.

**Knowing where a learned method applies.**

A learned method is useful only while its output respects the design constraints
and the conditions supported by its data and checks.

- **How can a generator enforce architecture constraints without collapsing
  useful design diversity?** Schemas, grammars, templates, and deterministic
  checks can exclude known illegal outputs. The hard part is preserving
  alternatives that matter while avoiding expensive evaluation of candidates
  that could never be accepted. Under a fixed candidate and checking budget, a
  useful evaluation reports the legal-output rate and validated coverage of
  distinct performance-cost regions rather than output count alone.

- **When does a sequential architecture problem justify a transition or world
  model?** Actions must change later state, and planning must save enough real
  evaluations to offset model error and checking cost. Reliable tests still
  need to distinguish those cases from problems where static prediction or
  direct tool feedback is sufficient. A discriminating protocol compares those
  alternatives under the same tool-call budget and reports decision quality,
  tool calls saved, and rollout error as the action horizon grows.

**Composing methods as the bottleneck moves.**

A composition must change when it moves rather than removes the limiting work.

- **How should an architecture team revise a method composition when the
  limiting work changes?** Generation can expose an evaluation bottleneck, and
  prediction can expose a review bottleneck. The challenge is to adapt without
  losing the external checks, cost accounting, fallback, and stopping
  conditions that made the earlier composition credible. An evaluation can
  induce a known shift in the active limit and measure detection delay, excess
  tool and review work, and decision quality at matched total cost.

## Conclusion

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Choose the smallest sufficient approach that preserves the check"}
Name the role before choosing an approach. Direct work or no added method may
be sufficient. When another component is needed, choose its family and
technique only after examining fit, and add components only when each performs
necessary work. Fit includes the question type, matching data conditions,
search structure, evaluator, total feedback cost, runtime and locality limits,
reliability, reversibility, and failure consequence. State the external check
that can reject the output; a generated checker is not automatically
independent.
:::

Prediction is useful when direct evaluation is too costly and observations
from matching workloads, design regions, tools, process conditions, and
representations can support an estimate. An architecture world model is one
transition-aware predictive technique, not a universal model of architecture.
Generation is useful when a required artifact or alternative is missing and an
external tool path can reject an invalid result. Optimization is useful when a
legal search space exceeds the evaluation budget; multiobjective optimization
can expose a Pareto frontier, but it cannot decide the architect's tradeoff.
Conventional techniques often provide the strongest practical implementation,
baseline, or fallback for these families.

These families do not impose a fixed order. Start with the missing capability,
then move among construction, estimation, selection, and direct evaluation as
feedback changes the work. Kernel generation requires an external compiler and
correctness harness, while compiler tuning may combine construction, a learned
cost model, search, compilation, and target measurement. The components and
their order are justified by the problem, not copied from a generic stack.

The selected approach now needs a tool-connected environment that preserves
its allowed changes, required tool roles, cost envelope, and necessary checks.
@sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces develops that environment.
